title: Jefferies Drops HDFC Bank, Adds MCX and Lenskart in India Portfolio Overhaul
excerpt: Christopher Wood's latest GREED & fear note reshapes Jefferies' India long-only portfolio, citing accelerating credit growth and strengthening macro tailwinds as reasons for a more constructive outlook on Indian equities.
body:
• Jefferies removed HDFC Bank and PB Fintech from its India long-only portfolio, replacing them with MCX and Lenskart Solutions.
  • REC was swapped for Bajaj Finance, and Eternal's allocation increased by one percentage point at Bharti Airtel's expense.
  • India's bank credit growth has accelerated to 17–18% year-on-year, the fastest pace in over a decade, led by corporate lending at roughly 20%.
  • Foreign investors bought a net $2.12 billion of Indian equities in July, though year-to-date outflows still total $25.86 billion.

Jefferies has overhauled its India long-only equity portfolio, dropping heavyweight HDFC Bank and adding commodity exchange MCX and eyewear retailer Lenskart Solutions, according to Christopher Wood's latest GREED & fear note published on Friday.

The reshuffle comes as Jefferies takes a more constructive view on India's domestic macro story, pointing to accelerating bank credit growth, returning foreign capital flows and policy measures supporting the rupee.

What Changed in the Portfolio

HDFC Bank, India's largest private lender and the heaviest stock in benchmark indexes such as the Nifty 50, was removed alongside PolicyBazaar-owner PB Fintech. MCX, India's leading multi-commodity exchange, and Lenskart Solutions, the fast-growing eyewear platform backed by SoftBank and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, replace them.

In a separate swap, infrastructure lender REC exits to make room for Bajaj Finance, one of India's dominant consumer lending franchises. Eternal, the parent company of food delivery platform Zomato, sees its allocation rise by one percentage point, funded by a reduction in telecom giant Bharti Airtel.

"There are some positives to be aware of as regards the Indian domestic story."

— Christopher Wood, Jefferies Global Head of Equity Strategy

Credit Growth Fuels Optimism

The key signal driving Jefferies' upgraded outlook is the acceleration in domestic bank lending. Credit growth has climbed to 17–18% year-on-year, the fastest pace in more than a decade, according to Wood's note. Corporate lending is expanding at approximately 20%, while loans to agriculture and retail borrowers are also growing at healthy rates — underscoring broad-based demand across the economy.

For a market that spent much of the past year grappling with foreign outflows and a weakening currency, the credit data suggests India's domestic growth engine is firing on multiple cylinders independent of global sentiment.

Foreign Flows and Rupee Recovery

Foreign investors returned as net buyers in July, purchasing $2.12 billion of Indian equities as India benefited from a global unwind of the memory chip trade, according to National Securities Depository data. However, they remain net sellers for 2026 overall, with cumulative outflows of $25.86 billion.

Policy-driven inflows are providing additional macro support. The Reserve Bank of India's foreign-currency inflow scheme — encompassing non-resident deposits, external commercial borrowings and foreign-currency bonds — had mobilized approximately $41 billion by the end of July. Jefferies expects total inflows under the scheme to reach $80 billion to $100 billion before the September 30 deadline.

A separate policy move, the removal of tax on interest income from foreign purchases of government bonds, has generated $8.7 billion in net inflows since early June, per exchange data.

The combined effect has stabilized the rupee, which recovered to 95.17 per U.S. dollar as of July 31 from a low of 96.96 in May.

Portfolio Implications

The portfolio changes reflect a shift toward domestic consumption and financial infrastructure plays. MCX benefits from rising commodity trading volumes and India's push to deepen its derivatives markets. Lenskart, which operates over 2,500 stores across India and Southeast Asia, represents a bet on India's growing consumer retail segment. Bajaj Finance, meanwhile, gives Jefferies exposure to India's consumer credit boom without the governance overhang that has dogged HDFC Bank since the resignation of its former chairman earlier this year.

HDFC Bank's removal is notable given Jefferies had only re-added the stock to its Asia ex-Japan portfolio in late 2024. The bank's shares have faced sustained pressure following the March resignation of part-time chairman Atanu Chakraborty, who cited differences with the bank over "values and ethics."

What to Watch

The durability of India's credit cycle and whether foreign inflows sustain through the September deadline for the RBI's forex scheme will be the key variables. If bank credit growth holds above 15% and the rupee remains stable, India's weight in global portfolios could continue to rise — a development that would benefit the new additions to Jefferies' India bet.
